summary: Specifies the Border Gateway Protocol, an inter-autonomous system routing protocol, together with its companion RFC 1164. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1267.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet is made of many separate networks. This is an early way for them to tell each other which places they can reach.

questions: how does bgp prevent routing loops
how does bgp connect autonomous systems
subtitle: An early protocol for exchanging routing information between independent networks.

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew, separate networks needed a way to tell each other how to reach their destinations, and to apply their own routing policies at the network boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: BGP establishes TCP connections between border routers and exchanges UPDATE messages describing which networks are reachable and which autonomous systems must be traversed to reach them.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1163 was the second version of BGP (historic) and was replaced by RFC 1267 (BGP version 3), which is itself now obsolete in favor of later versions.

today: RFC 1163 is Historic and was superseded by RFC 1267 (BGP version 3). Modern BGP is defined in RFC 4271 and later.

sections.title: Autonomous Systems and the Need for BGP
sections.content:
The Internet is divided into many Autonomous Systems (ASs): independent networks under single technical administration, each using its own interior routing protocol. BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the protocol by which these autonomous systems exchange reachability information with each other at the network boundaries.

The key innovation of BGP is that it does not just advertise routes; it advertises the full path of autonomous systems that traffic must traverse to reach a destination. This path information allows each AS to detect routing loops (if its own AS number appears in the path, there is a loop) and to apply policy decisions. For example, one AS might prefer routes through a particular neighbor over others, and BGP lets it express and enforce these preferences.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine each company's network is a building. BGP is like the security guards at the front door telling each other: "to get to the Johnson building, you go through the Smith building first".

sections.title: Message Types and Header Format
sections.content:
BGP runs over TCP on port 179 and uses four message types. All messages start with a 19-octet header containing a 16-octet Marker field (used for authentication and synchronization), a 2-octet Length, and a 1-octet Type code.

OPEN is the first message sent after a TCP connection is established. It contains the sender's AS number, a hold time (maximum seconds between successive messages), and an authentication code and data (defaulting to zero-length, meaning no authentication). UPDATE carries routing information: path attributes (such as ORIGIN, AS_PATH, and NEXT_HOP) followed by lists of network addresses. KEEPALIVE is a 19-octet message with no data, sent periodically to maintain liveness. NOTIFICATION reports an error and closes the connection immediately after being sent.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP talks like a polite conversation: "Hello, I am network 65001" (OPEN), then "I can reach these networks" (UPDATE), then "are you still there?" (KEEPALIVE), or "something went wrong" (NOTIFICATION).

sections.title: Path Attributes and Routing Information
sections.content:
Every UPDATE message carries path attributes that describe the route to a set of networks. The most important attributes are mandatory and well-known: ORIGIN (whether the route originated inside the AS, via EGP, or by other means), AS_PATH (the sequence of AS numbers traversed), and NEXT_HOP (the IP address of the border router to use as next hop).

Additional attributes include UNREACHABLE (marking previously advertised routes as no longer reachable) and optional attributes such as INTER-AS METRIC (a preference value for choosing among multiple exit points). Attributes are labeled as mandatory or discretionary, and as transitive (passed along to peers) or non-transitive (discarded by intermediate ASs). This structure allows BGP to be extended with new attributes without breaking older implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Each route has a label that says "I came from inside our AS" or "I learned this from EGP", and "to reach this network, go through AS 65001 then AS 65002". Newer implementations can add more labels, and older ones just ignore the new ones.

sections.title: Connection Management and Finite State Machine
sections.content:
BGP manages connections through a six-state finite state machine. Idle is the initial state; the system listens and allocates no resources until a Start event. Connect waits for the TCP connection to be established. Active attempts to initiate a TCP connection or awaits one from a peer. OpenSent waits for an OPEN message in reply to the one it sent; if the OPEN is acceptable, it sends KEEPALIVE and moves to OpenConfirm. OpenConfirm waits for a KEEPALIVE from the peer. Once received, the connection reaches Established state, where UPDATE, KEEPALIVE, and NOTIFICATION messages are exchanged.

If any error occurs, a NOTIFICATION is sent and the connection returns to Idle. Errors include message header problems, OPEN message rejections (unsupported version, bad AS number, authentication failure), UPDATE message problems (malformed attributes, missing mandatory attributes, AS loops), and hold timer expiry.
sections.plainLanguage: The two routers shake hands: "I am AS 65001" (OPEN), "OK, I hear you" (KEEPALIVE), then they talk (UPDATE). If either one stops talking for too long, they hang up and try again.

sections.title: Routing Policy and Loop Prevention
sections.content:
A core principle of BGP is that an AS advertises to its neighbors only the routes it itself uses. This enforces a "hop-by-hop" routing paradigm and prevents routing loops at the inter-AS level. When an UPDATE is propagated over an external (inter-AS) link, the local AS number is prepended to the AS_PATH attribute, building up the path as the route moves across the Internet.

Loop detection is simple: an AS checks whether its own AS number appears in the AS_PATH of an incoming route. If it does, that route is discarded (since following it would create a loop). This check prevents the most obvious routing loops. Beyond this, the RFC notes that enforcing consistent routing policies across all ASs is outside the scope of BGP itself: that is left to administrative coordination.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network adds its own name to the path when passing the route along: "go through us to reach that destination". If your name is already there, someone is trying to route traffic in a circle, so you ignore it.

fields.name: Marker
fields.desc: 16-octet field; all ones for OPEN, or computed from authentication mechanism.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total message length including header, in octets; range 19 to 4096.
